questions.q: What are the five standard stages of a plot in a narrative? List them in order.
questions.a: The five stages are: 1) Exposition (introduction of setting, characters, situation), 2) Rising Action (events that build tension), 3) Climax (turning point, highest tension), 4) Falling Action (events after climax leading to resolution), 5) Resolution (outcome). A wrong answer (e.g., missing stages or wrong order) reveals the student lacks the basic vocabulary to analyze plot structure.

questions.q: In "viw osQ lkFk <kbZ lky", the author narrates the story as an adult recalling childhood events. How does this first-person retrospective point of view affect the narrative structure? Explain in your own words.
questions.a: The retrospective narration allows the author to interject adult reflections, create dramatic irony (the child doesn't know what the adult knows), and structure the story thematically rather than strictly chronologically. A wrong answer (e.g., "it makes it more interesting") shows the student cannot analyze how point of view shapes structure.

questions.q: Identify the climax of the story and explain why it is the turning point. Use one specific detail from the text.
questions.a: The climax is the performance night when two actors appear as "Hkwyks" (the same character), causing confusion and comedy. This is the turning point because the play's success hangs on this moment, and the author's childhood dream is both realized and subverted. A wrong answer (e.g., identifying the stage-building as climax) shows the student cannot distinguish between rising action and climax.

questions.q: Compare the structure of the play within the story (the play being staged) with the structure of the story itself. How do they mirror each other?
questions.a: Both have a preparation phase (rehearsals/exposition), a performance (climax), and an aftermath (resolution). The story's narrative structure mimics the play's three-act structure, and the author's adult narration acts like a narrator in a play, commenting on the action. A weak answer fails to see the meta-theatrical parallel.

questions.q: Evaluate the author's decision to include the episode of the "Hkwyks" mix-up. Does it strengthen or weaken the narrative? Justify your opinion.
questions.a: It strengthens the narrative because it adds humor, highlights the theme of imperfection in art, and provides a memorable climax that underscores the community's collaborative spirit. A wrong evaluation (e.g., "it's just a funny incident") shows the student cannot link a plot event to thematic significance.

questions.q: Write a brief alternative ending (3-4 sentences) for the story where the play is a complete disaster, and explain how this would change the story's message.
questions.a: Alternative ending: The stage collapses, actors forget lines, and the audience leaves angry. The author feels shame and gives up theatre. This would change the message from "art brings community together despite flaws" to "failure destroys dreams." A poor answer would not connect the ending to the theme.
